result: The authors developed multiplexed reporter assays for Gs (cAMP) and Gq (calcium) signaling functions of MC4R in human HEK293T cells. The Gs assay was adapted from prior work, while the Gq assay required a novel 'relay' system using Gal4-VPR transcriptional activator to amplify signal. Both assays provide sensitive functional readouts for MC4R signaling activities.
evaluation: Claims C38-C50 describe the development and validation of the reporter assays with detailed methodology and supporting data in Figure 1 and supplements. The relay system design for Gq signaling is well-documented and addresses the weak signal-to-noise issue. The assays are demonstrated to produce dose-dependent responses to α-MSH stimulation.

result: The authors developed a mixed-effect negative binomial GLM for DMS analysis that leverages barcode information and supports hypothesis testing between conditions. They optimized protocols to achieve ~30 barcodes per variant (vs. ~10 in prior work), which increased statistical power to detect variant effects, as demonstrated by improved separation of stop codon variants from missense variants and reduced standard errors.
evaluation: Claims C52-C60 describe methodological improvements with clear statistical justification. The negative binomial model is appropriate for overdispersed count data from RNA-seq. The downsampling analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) directly demonstrates that increased barcodes reduce standard errors as expected. The comparison with β2AR data shows substantial improvement in signal separation.

result: The study performed comprehensive DMS of MC4R, testing 6,633 of 6,640 possible single amino acid substitutions (99.9% coverage) across 18 experimental conditions in quadruplicate. Each variant was represented by an average of 56 and 28 barcodes for Gs and Gq pathways respectively, resulting in >557,000 uniquely engineered cells and >21,500,000 total measurements.
evaluation: Claims C3, C5, C6, C29, C61-C66 provide specific quantitative details about the experimental scale that are internally consistent and supported by the data presented. The calculations for total measurements are verifiable from the stated parameters (6,633 variants × 18 conditions × 4 replicates × average barcodes per variant). The 99.9% variant coverage is exceptional for DMS studies.

result: The DMS data accurately assess MC4R variant effects, as validated by multiple benchmarks: variants in transmembrane domains and stop codons are predominantly loss-of-function; 63.3% of ClinVar pathogenic variants show significant loss of Gs signaling; loss-of-function variants are rarer in human populations; 93.4% of DMS loss-of-function variants are predicted deleterious by AlphaMissense; results correlate with literature classifications (Pearson r=0.84 with Zhang et al. 2021 data).
evaluation: Claims C67-C74 present multiple independent validations of the DMS data quality. The convergence of evidence from structural expectations, clinical databases (ClinVar), population genetics (gnomAD), computational predictors (AlphaMissense, popEVE), and published experimental data provides strong support. The quantitative correlations are substantial (r=0.84, R²=0.71) and the agreement with categorical classifications is high.

result: Different experimental conditions have distinct capabilities for detecting loss-of-function versus gain-of-function variants. Unstimulated conditions identify constitutively active variants but poorly detect loss-of-function, while agonist-stimulated conditions effectively identify loss-of-function. Across all α-MSH conditions, 50.8% of variants are loss-of-function in at least one condition, 5.2% are gain-of-function, 45.2% show wild-type activity, and 1.2% are context-dependent (both LoF and GoF depending on condition).
evaluation: Claims C75-C82 describe condition-dependent variant effects with specific quantitative data shown in Figure 2G. The observation that different conditions detect different functional classes is logical and well-supported. The identification of 80 variants (1.2%) that are both LoF and GoF depending on condition is particularly interesting and demonstrates the value of multi-condition testing.

result: The study provides functional classifications for 220 human MC4R variants from ClinVar and patient studies. Of these, 59.1% are loss-of-function in at least one condition. Among ClinVar-classified variants, 83.9% of pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants are LoF, 53.3% of VUS/conflicting variants are LoF, and 0% of benign variants are LoF. Three variants (V103I, H158R, I251L) show gain-of-function consistent with protective effects.
evaluation: Claims C83-C89 present systematic variant interpretation with clear quantitative results provided in Supplementary file 1b. The high concordance with ClinVar pathogenic classifications (83.9%) and complete concordance with benign classifications (0% LoF) validates the approach. The identification of protective GoF variants is supported by literature citations.

result: PCA analysis across eight DMS datasets (Gs and Gq at four α-MSH doses) identified variants that differentially affect Gs versus Gq signaling. PC1 (66% variance) separates variants by overall effect on function, while PC2 (12% variance) separates pathway-biased variants. Variants with high PC2 show Gq bias (increased Gq, normal Gs), while negative PC2 indicates Gs bias (normal Gs, reduced Gq). More variants increase Gq than Gs signaling, and biased variants are positionally diverse across MC4R structure.
evaluation: Claims C7, C32, C92-C103 describe the PCA analysis and identification of biased variants with clear support from Figure 3 and supplements. The variance explained by PC1 and PC2 is substantial (78% total). The interpretation that PC2 captures pathway bias is well-supported by the data patterns shown. The observation that biased variants are positionally diverse (14 extreme Gq-biased variants at 12 positions) is specific and verifiable.

result: The study identified specific biased variants within the MC4R signaling cascade and G-protein binding regions. Gq-biased variants include I137L, F254P, L140I in the signaling cascade core, and T150G, H158R in the G-protein binding pocket. The H158R variant, found in humans, was previously shown to preferentially signal through Gq. Novel potentially biased positions include M79 (multiple Gq-biased variants: M79R, M79S, M79G), I223L (most extreme bias), and V228R, which interface with Gαs.
evaluation: Claims C104-C122 integrate DMS data with structural knowledge to identify and interpret biased variants. The identification of specific variants is supported by Figure 3 and supplements. The connection to prior literature (H158R previously shown to be Gq-biased) validates the approach. The structural interpretations are reasonable given the known MC4R activation mechanism and G-protein interfaces, though some novel interactions would benefit from experimental validation.

result: The study tested whether Ipsen 17 (a small molecule corrector) could restore Gs signaling function of MC4R variants. Of 6,633 tested variants, 290 (4.4%) showed disrupted Gs signaling that was partially or fully rescued by Ipsen 17. Rescued variants include pathogenic variants from ClinVar and patient studies, while other patient variants showed no response to corrector therapy.
evaluation: Claims C9, C33, C130-C135 describe the corrector experiments with specific quantitative results shown in Figure 4 and supplement. The identification of 290 responsive variants (4.4%) is a concrete finding. The demonstration that some clinically relevant variants respond while others do not is important for potential therapeutic stratification. The statistical analysis methods for defining 'rescue' are described in the methods section.

result: Bayesian meta-regression analysis comparing α-MSH and THIQ stimulation (at low doses, FDR<5%) identified variants that uniquely disrupt activation by one ligand but not the other. These variants cluster in the orthosteric binding pocket. More variants uniquely disrupt α-MSH than THIQ, consistent with the peptide using a larger interaction network. Specific examples include position I104 (most substitutions disrupt α-MSH but not THIQ), P48 (most substitutions disrupt α-MSH, but P48D uniquely disrupts THIQ), and I129 (polar substitutions disrupt THIQ, I129V disrupts α-MSH).
evaluation: Claims C10, C34, C140-C149, C152-C153, C155-C157 describe ligand-specific effects with detailed support from Figure 5. The Bayesian meta-regression approach is appropriate for comparing ligand effects while accounting for systematic differences. The clustering of ligand-specific variants in the orthosteric pocket is expected and validates the approach. The specific examples at positions 48, 104, and 129 are well-documented with structural context. The interpretations are consistent with known structural differences between peptide and small molecule binding.

result: The study demonstrates improved DMS methods enable quantitative, disease-relevant measurements for drug discovery applications. Key achievements include: quantifying differences in Gs and Gq signaling for MC4R, systematically assessing corrector therapy responses, identifying biased signaling variants, and elucidating protein-ligand interaction differences between peptide and small molecule agonists. These capabilities address critical needs in precision medicine and drug development.
evaluation: Claims C28, C30-C31, C159-C161, C163, C168-C171 summarize the major contributions and their significance. These summary claims are well-supported by the specific results described in other claim groups. The study successfully demonstrates multiple drug discovery applications of improved DMS methods. The quantitative nature of the measurements and the disease relevance (MC4R in obesity) are clear strengths.

result: The introduction establishes the context for DMS in drug discovery: DMS is an emerging method for systematically testing variant effects; it has been used for various protein functions and human variant interpretation; applications in drug discovery require more disease-relevant, sensitive, and quantitative methods than currently available; MC4R is a medically relevant GPCR target where loss-of-function variants cause inherited obesity and agonists are being developed as therapeutics.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C12-C27, C35-C37 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These are primarily literature review claims establishing the rationale for the study. The characterization of current DMS limitations (C16-C18) and the potential for drug discovery applications (C19-C22) are reasonable assessments supported by citations. The background on MC4R (C25-C27, C37) is well-established knowledge.

result: The HFRW motif (His6-Phe7-Arg8-Trp9) of α-MSH represents a conserved pharmacophore critical for MC4R activation by peptides. The tri-branched THIQ molecule (R1-R2-R3) mimics the HFRW conformational architecture. The Phe7 of α-MSH and analogous R2 group of THIQ form key interactions with Ca2+ and the hydrophobic pocket formed by I129 of MC4R.
evaluation: Claims C150-C151, C154 describe established structural knowledge about MC4R ligands supported by multiple citations (Gonçalves et al., 2018; Hruby et al., 1987; Zhang et al., 2021). This background information provides context for interpreting the DMS results on ligand-specific effects.

result: Background on MC4R signaling and therapeutic strategies: MC4R signals through multiple G-protein pathways; biasing activity toward specific pathways could be therapeutically valuable; many MC4R variants cause misfolding; corrector therapies have been developed for other diseases and proposed for MC4R-associated obesity; correctors are typically effective only for specific variants; substantial work has characterized peptide agonist interactions with MC4R, but small molecule agonist characterization is limited; Gq bias is a purported mechanism for Setmelanotide's better side-effect profile.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91, C99, C123-C129, C138-C139, C162 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for studying biased signaling, corrector therapy, and ligand-specific interactions. The information is well-established in the literature.

result: Justification for the analytical approach: Most popular DMS analysis methods do not leverage barcodes or support hypothesis testing between conditions; summing barcodes within variants sacrifices statistical power; DMS counts are expected to be overdispersed since the reporter system uses RNA-seq readout; mixed-effects negative binomial GLMs have been widely used for RNA-seq differential expression analysis.
evaluation: Claims C51, C202-C204 provide methodological justification supported by citations. The critique of existing methods is reasonable and the choice of negative binomial model is well-justified given the RNA-seq readout and expected overdispersion. The connection to established RNA-seq analysis methods is appropriate.

result: Detailed methods for reporter assays, library construction, variant-barcode mapping, DMS assay execution, sequencing, statistical analysis, data sources, PCA analysis, corrector response analysis, ligand comparison analysis, structural visualization, and cell line validation. Key metrics include: median 8-10 reads per barcode, median 28-56 barcodes per variant, replicate correlation r~0.4-0.5, 30-60× cellular coverage per variant.
evaluation: Claims C182-C220 provide comprehensive methodological details with appropriate citations and specific quantitative parameters. The methods are generally well-described and reproducible. The quality control metrics (barcode purity >0.75, read depth >10, replicate correlations) are reasonable. The statistical approaches (negative binomial GLM, Benjamini-Hochberg correction, Bayesian meta-regression) are appropriate for the data types and questions.

result: Discussion of future applications and broader impact: The identified biased variants could be used to design drugs that selectively bias MC4R activity; DMS is a powerful method for drug discovery; DMS tests all variants in one experiment (vs. traditional one-at-a-time approaches); DMS could enable understanding treatment responses across populations before clinical trials; the methods are broadly applicable to GPCRs and other target classes; DMS data could help identify novel binding pockets and optimize compounds; machine learning models have struggled with real-world disease applications, possibly due to limitations in training data; high-quality DMS data will be critical for developing better models.
evaluation: Claims C8, C11, C164-C167, C172-C181 are primarily forward-looking statements about potential applications and future impact. While the underlying DMS data are solid, these claims about future utility are speculative. The potential for drug design based on biased variants (C8) is reasonable but unproven. The critique of machine learning models (C178-C179) is supported by citation but the hypothesis about training data limitations is speculative. The claim about broad applicability (C174-C176) is plausible but not directly demonstrated.
